children: East Africa’s smaller airlines are bearing the brunt of the Iran war as the continent’s bigger carriers report increased passenger numbers and revenues, with weaker passenger demand, suspended Gulf routes and soaring fuel costs forcing them to cut capacity and rethink schedules.

RwandAir has disclosed that it was forced to suspend flights to Dubai and Doha after the conflict disrupted airspace in the Middle East, while its cargo operations to Dubai, Sharjah and Abu Dhabi, which are key routes for its cargo operations were also affected.

The Rwandan flag carrier’s Chief Executive Yvonne Makolo, speaking at the Aviation Africa Summit in Nairobi this week, said the disruption also caused its fuel costs to surge by over 70 percent, and now accounts for more than 40 percent of RwandAir’s costs.“Fuel as a percentage of our costs is over 40 percent, so that’s a big impact for a relatively small airline like us,” Ms Makolo said.

Kenya’s budget carrier, Jambojet, also says the conflict significantly impacted its operations, with dampened demand forcing it to reduce its available capacity has felt the shock mainly through weaker passenger demand.

Karanja Ndegwa, Jambojet CEO said it responded to the reduced traffic on its key routes by reducing capacity, including by cutting frequencies on some of its routes, to avoid operating flights with significantly lower load factors.“This proactive action helped us manage costs by reducing variable operating expenses such as fuel and other flight-related costs, while ensuring that our capacity remained aligned with actual market demand,” Mr Ndegwa told The EastAfrican on the sidelines of the summit.
Jambojet has since seen demand and load factors improve, prompting it to deploy more capacity across its network.
The carrier also faced a steep increase in fuel costs. Mr Ndegwa said fuel’s share of total costs rose from about 18 percent to 34 percent following the disruption.

The experience contrasts with the performance of the region’s larger network airlines, which have been better placed to absorb the shock by capturing travellers rerouted through Africa after the disruptions in the Middle East.

Kenya Airways reported a 9 percent increase in first-half revenue to Ksh81 billion ($626 million) despite operating 9 percent less capacity. Its cabin factor improved by four percentage points, while stronger average fares also supported revenue growth. The gains, however, did not translate into profitability. KQ’s fuel costs rose 66 percent during the period, while the airline reported a Ksh16 billion ($124 million) pre-tax loss, up from Ksh12.17 billion ($94 million) a year earlier.

Ethiopian Airlines has similarly continued to expand despite the geopolitical shock. The carrier reported a 20 percent increase in annual revenue to $9.1 billion for the year ended June, while passenger traffic rose 8 percent to 20.7 million. Cargo volumes increased 16 percent to 897,000 tonnes.

The difference highlights the vulnerability of smaller carriers to shocks concentrated around individual markets. Other smaller carriers on the continent, including Asky and Astral Aviation, also reported a significant impact on their operations.

The conflict has also raised costs across the industry. African airlines have faced higher jet-fuel prices and longer or altered flight paths as carriers avoid affected airspace. Kenya Airways, for example, has said some rerouted flights require substantially more fuel.

title: ZAWYA: East Africa’s small airlines hit hard by Iran conflict
